prompt.brief: Design a customer identity platform for registration, social login, MFA, consent, conditional access, account recovery, and token issuance across multiple applications and tenants.
successSignals: Define the customer profile, verified identifiers, linked social identities, MFA factors, sessions, consent, risk, and tenant boundaries.
Design secure journeys for signup, verification, login, recovery, consent, step-up MFA, account linking, and conditional access.
Separate durable identity records from tokens, risk signals, notifications, and application claims; make external-provider retries safe.
Explain enumeration resistance, credential abuse, key rotation, privacy deletion, auditability, regional recovery, and degraded behavior.

functional: Register and verify customers, authenticate local or social identities, issue tokens, enforce MFA/conditional access, and manage sessions.
Support account linking, password reset, factor enrollment/revocation, consent, profile updates, logout-all, and application claims.
Provide tenant isolation, audit events, deletion/export, provider outage handling, risk challenges, and idempotent recovery flows.
nonFunctional: Meet p95 token issuance under 500ms for healthy dependencies and fail closed for uncertain authorization decisions.
Scale to 50M customers and login bursts without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 50M customers, 10k tenants, and 25k authentication attempts per second at peak
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

architecture.title: Secure Identity Management Solution control-plane architecture
architecture.summary: Design a customer identity platform for registration, social login, MFA, consent, conditional access, account recovery, and token issuance across multiple applications and tenants. The design separates versioned desired state from leased reconciliation work and provider mutations, making drift, retries, approvals, and audit history explicit.

deepDives.title: Desired versus observed state
points: Keep secure identity management solution desired state separate from provider-observed state and show both to operators.
Make every reconciliation step conditional and resumable so a worker crash does not restart unsafe effects.
Version policy and resource state so old operations cannot overwrite newer intent.

deepDives.title: Provider failures and unknown outcomes
points: Use provider-specific idempotency tokens and query-after-timeout behavior for secure identity management solution operations.
Bound retries with exponential backoff, circuit breakers, and per-provider quotas.
Route irreconcilable drift to an approval or quarantine path instead of retrying forever.

deepDives.title: Blast radius and operations
points: Partition secure identity management solution work by tenant, region, cluster, or resource class and cap concurrent mutations.
Audit who changed desired state, which policy allowed it, and what provider evidence was observed.
Alert on drift age, operation backlog, failed steps, policy denials, and stale observations.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull reconciliation
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use event triggers for fast response and periodic scans for missed events, drift, and recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: A push-only secure identity management solution controller silently misses changes when a provider event is lost.

tradeoffs.title: Central control plane versus provider-native controllers
tradeoffs.recommendation: Keep policy, intent, and audit centralized while isolating provider-specific application logic behind adapters.
tradeoffs.caution: A monolithic controller becomes hard to scale and couples unrelated provider failure domains.

tradeoffs.title: Automatic repair versus approval
tradeoffs.recommendation: Automate low-risk, reversible secure identity management solution changes and require approval for destructive or high-blast-radius operations.
tradeoffs.caution: Full automation without policy or blast-radius controls can turn a transient signal into a widespread outage.

commonMistakes: Treating a secure identity management solution API response as proof that the provider has reached the desired state.
Overwriting desired state with stale observed state after an out-of-order worker response.
Retrying timed-out provider mutations without an idempotency token or status lookup.
Running every tenant or region through one queue and allowing a hot failure domain to block all work.
Omitting policy version, operator identity, provider evidence, and drift age from the audit trail.

followUps.question: How do you handle a secure identity management solution provider timeout?
followUps.answer: Persist the operation as unknown, query provider state using the idempotency token, and only retry or compensate after the result is known.

followUps.question: How do you stop a bad rollout?
followUps.answer: Use policy gates, concurrency limits, canary scopes, operation cancellation, and a versioned last-known-good desired state.

followUps.question: How do you detect drift?
followUps.answer: Compare periodic provider observations with desired state, record the observed version and age, and route policy-compliant repair separately from manual exceptions.
